query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning–driven predictive model, integrated with detailed thermal processing data, can be used to control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or conventionally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA exhibiting a multi‐phase microstructure with both desired and undesired phases.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a data‐driven machine learning model to design optimized heat treatment schedules (including precise annealing and controlled cooling protocols) tailored to tune phase transformations.
generation.conditions: Well‐controlled temperature–time profiles, specific cooling rates, and an appropriate processing atmosphere to reliably trigger targeted phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and distribution of phases and precipitates (such as coherent strengthening domains) that evolve in response to the optimized thermal processing.
generation.mechanism: The ML model integrates extensive processing parameters and microstructural characterization data to decode complex phase transformation kinetics. It predicts optimal thermal profiles that promote desirable phase assemblages and suppress unwanted transformations by adjusting nucleation and growth rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: A more homogeneous microstructure with controlled precipitate size and distribution, resulting in improved mechanical and functional properties compared to conventional heat treatments.
generation.baseline: Conventional thermal processing methods which adjust only global thermal profiles and often result in coarse, inhomogeneous phase distributions.
generation.boundary: This approach’s success depends on the quality and comprehensiveness of the training data, and it may be less predictive when novel or unforeseen transformation pathways occur in these complex alloys.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the quantitative prediction of phase kinetics and the extent to which the ML model can generalize across all processing conditions in the multiphase HEA system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples with identical initial conditions. Process one set using a conventional thermal treatment schedule and process the other set using the ML-recommended optimized heat treatment. Characterize both sets using standard phase identification and mechanical testing.
measurements: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructure and precipitate morphology
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) for phase transformation temperatures
Mechanical tests (e.g., tensile strength, ductility) for performance assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-guided treatment does not produce statistically significant improvements in phase homogeneity, target phase volume fraction, or enhanced mechanical properties compared to the conventional processing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), as a novel type of material generally consisting of five or more principle elements, have attracted extensive attention in recent years because of their attractive crystallographic and mechanical properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Although it is anticipated that simple solid solution phases are easier to form rather than the intermetallic compounds or complex-ordered phases due to their high configurational entropy [ [8] , [9] ], only a few HEAs have exactly single and stable solid solution structures, among which CoCrFeNiMn alloy is widely concerned [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. It possesses a single face-center-cubic (fcc) solid solution phase even after a series of thermomechanical processing [ [15] , [16] ] and its constituent elements have more sluggish diffusion compared to other conventional alloys [ [17] ]. These characterizations contribute to excellent mechanical properties with a satisfactory combination between tensile strength and ductility [ [18] , [19] ]. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

decision.trend: Initial studies on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys explored how thermal processing (annealing at different temperatures, controlled cooling, even high-pressure treatments) affects phase evolution and precipitation behavior. Researchers demonstrated that processing parameters strongly influence the onset, growth, and coherence of precipitates within multiphase microstructures. However, despite these experimental advances, the complex interplay of multiple competing phase transformation pathways has kept precise control elusive.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to reliably predict and finely tune the phase evolution in these complex alloys. Because conventional heat treatment methods adjust only global thermal profiles, they often cannot cope with the sensitive and intertwined kinetics of various phases in a multiphase HEA system.
decision.lever: Developing a predictive model that integrates detailed processing parameters (e.g., temperature–time profiles, cooling rates) and microstructural characterization data to forecast phase transformation pathways and optimize heat treatment schedules
decision.why: A data-driven approach can harness extensive experimental datasets to decode the complex relationships between thermal parameters and phase evolution. This method directly addresses the limitations of conventional processing by providing a systematic way to predict and control multiphase transformation in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
